content: Mouth ulcers are defined as sores or open lesions that occur within the oral cavity. Symptoms of Mouth Ulcers The symptoms of mouth ulcers can vary depending on the underlying cause. Common symptoms include: Open sores in the mouth. Pain or discomfort localized to the affected area. Causes of Mouth Ulcers Mouth ulcers can arise from a variety of conditions, including: Canker sores (aphthous ulcers). Gingivostomatitis. Herpes simplex virus infections (commonly presenting as fever blisters). Leukoplakia. Oral cancer. Oral lichen planus. Oral thrush (candidiasis). Additionally, histoplasmosis, a fungal infection, may manifest as skin lesions that appear as mouth ulcers. High-Risk Groups Individuals with the following conditions are at an increased risk of developing mouth ulcers: Canker sores. Gingivostomatitis. Herpes simplex virus infections. Leukoplakia. Oral cancer. Oral lichen planus. Oral thrush. Diagnosis Healthcare providers or dentists typically diagnose mouth ulcers based on their appearance and location within the oral cavity. In some cases, blood tests or a biopsy of the ulcer may be required to confirm the underlying cause. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your healthcare provider if: Your mouth ulcers persist for more than three weeks without improvement. You experience frequent recurrences of mouth ulcers. New symptoms develop alongside the ulcers. Treatment Options The primary goal of treatment is to alleviate symptoms. If the underlying cause is identified, it should be addressed directly. Maintaining gentle and thorough oral hygiene can help reduce symptoms. Topical treatments, such as antihistamines, antacids, corticosteroids, or other soothing preparations, may be applied directly to the ulcer. Avoid consuming hot or spicy foods, as they can exacerbate the pain associated with mouth ulcers. Prognosis The prognosis for mouth ulcers depends on their underlying cause. Many mouth ulcers are benign and resolve without treatment. However, certain types of cancer, such as squamous cell carcinoma, may initially present as a non-healing mouth ulcer. Possible Complications Complications associated with mouth ulcers include: Cellulitis of the mouth, resulting from secondary bacterial infection of the ulcers. Dental infections, such as tooth abscesses. Oral cancer. Transmission of contagious conditions to others. Prevention Good oral hygiene practices can help prevent certain types of mouth ulcers and reduce the risk of complications. These practices include: Brushing teeth at least twice daily. Flossing at least once daily. Regular professional dental cleanings and examinations.
